item.title: Taiwan analysts say Trump-Xi summit produced no policy shift but real test lies ahead
item.description: Taiwan analysts assess whether Xi Jinping secured private concessions from Trump, with arms sales and senior U.S. official visits as key tests ahead.
item.content:encoded:
TAIPEI — Taiwanese officials were watching carefully for signs of policy changes toward the island as President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit last week in Washington D.C.

Xi’s visit was of high interest in Taiwan, a regular target of China’s threats. On Saturday, a panel that included scholars, a retired U.S. military officer, and Taiwan’s deputy foreign minister at the Institute for National Policy Research (INPR) in Taipei assessed what the third Trump–Xi meeting of Trump’s current term means for Taiwan. Most expect no change in U.S. policy toward Taiwan.

"Both of them got what they want and what they need," Kuo Yu-jen, INPR’s vice president and a professor at National Sun Yat-sen University’s Institute of China and Asia-Pacific Studies, told Fox News Digital. Trump can point to economic results from negotiating with Xi, while Xi can return to Beijing with the prestige of a high-profile U.S. reception, Kuo said. He called claims by some that Trump had "sold out" Taiwan excessive speculation.

XI PRAISES US STATE VISIT 'PERFECTION' AS TRUMP CALLS MEETINGS 'VERY PRODUCTIVE'

As expected, Xi reportedly pressed Trump to say the United States opposes Taiwan independence. Washington’s preferred description is that it does not support Taiwan independence, a distinction that, much to the relief of Taiwan government officials, Trump maintained.

Speaking exclusively to Fox News Digital after the forum, Taiwan’s Deputy Foreign Minister François Wu said Beijing wants more than a change in diplomatic language. It wants the world to view Taiwan as a domestic Chinese issue. If that argument succeeds, Wu said, Beijing could claim other countries have no right to respond to its actions against the island.

"The so-called independence of Taiwan is just an issue made specifically by the Chinese government," Wu said. Taiwan already has a president and government elected by its people, territory and its own currency, he said. "We just don’t need to declare any independence. We are a sovereign country."

Wu had expressed concerns prior to Trump’s visit to China in May, when he told Bloomberg that "What we are most afraid of is to put Taiwan on the menu of the talk between Xi Jinping and President Trump."

China’s Foreign Ministry claims Xi urged Trump to maintain the "correct position" to oppose Taiwan independence. Taiwan’s Foreign Ministry rushed out an objection on a public holiday in Taiwan, and repeated Taiwan’s own clear position on its sovereignty.

CHINA DEPLOYED OVER 100 VESSELS NEAR TAIWAN IN THE WAKE OF TRUMP-XI SUMMIT, TAIWAN SECURITY OFFICIAL CLAIMS

The White House summary of Xi’s visit announced no change in Taiwan policy and instead emphasized more favorable tariff treatment for US$30 billion in goods in each direction, an AI incident communication channel and U.S. concerns about rare earth and critical-mineral supplies.

The visit nonetheless raised questions in Taiwan about what Xi might have obtained from Trump in private. Analysts cautioned that if there was a deal over Taiwan, it would only become clear in the coming months. Taiwan awaits Trump’s approval for more arms sales, visits to Taiwan by senior U.S. officials and a potential transit stop in the U.S. for Taiwan’s president. China objects to all of these, so how Trump handles them must balance relations with China, maintaining support for Taiwan and Trump’s priorities.

Dong Li-wen, executive director of the government-funded Foundation on Asia-Pacific Peace Studies, described the leaders’ shared approach as delaying difficult decisions while waiting for circumstances to change. For Xi, Dong argued, that is a longer-term strategy. For Trump, it is a temporary tactic. The two sides can keep talking and set aside issues they cannot settle, but their underlying competition remains.

The argument over Taiwan’s status is almost 80 years old. China claims the island as its territory, but the People’s Republic of China has not governed it for even a single day. The Republic of China government relocated to Taiwan after the Chinese Nationalists lost the civil war to Mao Zedong’s Communists in 1949.

The governing Democratic Progressive Party’s 1999 Resolution on Taiwan’s Future described Taiwan as an independent sovereign state called the Republic of China under its existing constitution. All of Taiwan’s democratically elected presidents have said something similar in interviews with international media, including Lee Teng-hui to The Washington Post in 1997, Chen Shui-bian to the BBC in 2010, Ma Ying-jeou to CNN in 2010, and Tsai Ing-wen to the BBC in 2020. Current President William Lai Ching-te said the same thing to Time in 2024, adding an oft-repeated insistence that the Republic of China and the People’s Republic of China are not subordinate to each other.

That status quo — which amounts to Taiwan being a de facto independent state — is what Taiwan intends to defend, according to Deputy Foreign Minister Wu. Xi left Washington having restated China’s demands. Analysts at the gathering said whether Xi managed to nudge U.S. policy in any way will soon be tested in decisions over arms sales and other issues, with some predicting weapons packages could be scaled down or "unbundled."

Speaking separately to Fox News Digital, Ross Darrell Feingold, a political analyst and assistant professor at Tamkang University’s Department of Diplomacy and International Relations, noted that with a local election in Taiwan this November, followed by presidential and legislative elections in January 2028, Taiwan’s domestic politics could also be a factor in U.S. decisions. "Although the U.S. is likely to back President Lai’s re-election; agreeing to arms sales, visits by Trump administration officials or Lai’s desired transit stop in the U.S. will need to be balanced against coming across as too blatantly interfering in Taiwan’s election, as well as the inevitable anger from China".

item.title: Brian Schottenheimer promises to improve as Jerry Jones flags Cowboys’ gaffes in late loss to Ravens in Brazil
item.description: Jerry Jones expressed deep frustration over the Dallas Cowboys' final 28 seconds against the Baltimore Ravens, saying no explanation is satisfying.
item.content:encoded:
Longtime Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones did little to hide his frustration with how the final seconds unfolded in Sunday’s improbable loss to the Baltimore Ravens in the NFL’s debut game in Rio de Janeiro.

After Dallas scored to tie the game at 31 in the final minute, Baltimore received the ensuing kickoff with just seven seconds remaining. The game appeared destined for overtime. Instead, Brandon Aubrey’s kickoff sailed into the end zone for a touchback, and Lamar Jackson’s 27-yard pass to Zay Flowers moved the Ravens into position for a game-winning field goal.

Jones and Schottenheimer retraced the offensive sequence that culminated in Brandon Aubrey’s 23-yard game-tying field goal, beginning with the playcalling after Dallas reached first-and-goal at the 2-yard line. They also examined Prescott’s third-down throwaway, which forced the Cowboys to settle for the tying kick.

Jones acknowledged that the Cowboys could not change what happened in the final seconds but said they could use the experience to avoid repeating the same mistakes.

"There is no explanation you're satisfied with. None," the longtime Cowboys general manager said during his latest appearance on Dallas radio station 105.3 The Fan.

JERRY JONES ISSUES 'DANGEROUS' WARNING AFTER COWBOYS TOPPLE COMMANDERS BEHIND DAK PRESCOTT'S HISTORIC DAY

"Let's be sure that we all understand that. [The coaches] don't have one that they're satisfied with. ... But there's an evaluation of how not to make the same mistakes again. You can't get that back. [There's] no way to get it back. What you can do is use it ... to get better. That's what's being done."

Schottenheimer struck a similar tone in his first public comments since the Cowboys returned to the U.S., acknowledging the mistakes, accepting responsibility and emphasizing his continued alignment with Jones.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I'm man enough to take mistakes. I make a lot of mistakes. I'm certainly not perfect," Schottenheimer said. "And I know one thing, Jerry and I had a very good conversation about it. I explained it. He understands. He understands that there was a mistake that was made, and he was terrific. Great, sound advice. I value him. He's been around the game a long time, just like I have, and he's seen a lot of stuff.

"And so to me, that shows that he and I are aligned very closely. This will make me better. I'll be better. And again, I'm looking forward to lining up and playing this week against the Texans."

Schottenheimer then turned the focus to his own performance, adding, "I hurt our chance to win that game and I'll be better. And I'm better than that. I'm better than I performed in the last 28 seconds."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Schottenheimer, the son of former NFL coach Marty Schottenheimer, said frustration over the third-down call influenced the kickoff decision, while communication between special teams coordinator Nick Sorensen and game management coordinator Ryan Feder also fell short.

"My dad had a rule — one play at a time," he said. "He talked a lot about it, because it happened to him. He made a decision on a play, it didn't go good, he was pissed off about it and it affected another decision. I think that's kind of what happened to me. So I'll take accountability for it. It's football and life. It's what happens."

Schottenheimer is just 20 games into his head-coaching career after spending a quarter-century on various NFL coaching staffs.

At 1-2 entering Week 4, the Cowboys will face the Houston Texans, Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Green Bay Packers over their next three games. The trio has combined for one win this season. Tampa Bay will also be without starting quarterback Baker Mayfield for the next few weeks, with undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels expected to fill in.

item.title: US military completes withdrawal of troops from Iraq after 12-year mission
item.description: The U.S. military completed its withdrawal from Erbil Air Base, ending Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq while relocating its headquarters to Jordan.
item.content:encoded:
The US military has completed the withdrawal of American forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base in Iraq, ending its Operation Inherent Resolve mission, US Central Command announced Wednesday.

The departure closes the Iraq chapter of the U.S.-led military mission launched against ISIS in 2014, while shifting primary responsibility for the country's security to Iraqi forces. The broader counter-ISIS campaign is not ending, however, with the U.S.-led task force relocating its headquarters to Jordan and operations continuing in Syria.

"Job well done to the tens of thousands of American service members, diplomats, and civilian personnel who answered the call in Iraq," CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said.

US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM

"Because of your grit, sacrifice and professionalism, ISIS no longer poses a systemic threat to Iraq’s national security and Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga and other Iraqi Kurdistan Region security forces, now possess the capacity, leadership, and operational independence to unilaterally manage threats to their homeland."

Erbil Air Base in northern Iraq served as the main operational hub for Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve and hosted most of the roughly 1,500 American and Coalition forces supporting counter-ISIS operations, according to CENTCOM.

U.S. and Coalition forces began leaving federal Iraq last October as Washington and Baghdad moved toward a bilateral defense relationship. The final removal of personnel and equipment from Erbil completed that transition on Sept. 30.

Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve remains active and is now headquartered in Jordan, according to CENTCOM. U.S. forces also continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria alongside Coalition partners and the Syrian government.

SYRIA OFF US TERROR BLACKLIST AFTER NEARLY 50 YEARS AS TRUMP ADMIN CLEARS INVESTMENT HURDLE

"As we step back and hand full primary responsibility for Iraq’s security to the Government of Iraq and the brave people of Iraq, U.S. and Coalition forces stationed across the region will remain ready to respond to any ISIS threats that arise," Cooper said.

"Maintaining our vigilance and readiness is essential to protecting the U.S. homeland and strengthening regional security," he added. 

The withdrawal ends a U.S. military presence in Iraq that was reestablished in 2014, when Iraqi authorities sought international assistance as ISIS captured large areas of the country. U.S. troops had previously left Iraq in 2011 following the 2003 invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein.

The final departure comes as Iraq faces a separate security challenge from powerful Iran-backed militias operating inside the country. Baghdad has sought to bring weapons held by non-state groups under government control, but some of the most influential militias have resisted disarming.

The withdrawal has drawn sharply different reactions inside Iraq. Iran-aligned groups celebrated the U.S. departure, while officials in the country's Kurdish region have raised concerns about the loss of American air-defense capabilities amid drone and missile threats.

CENTCOM said U.S. and Coalition forces elsewhere in the region will remain prepared to respond if ISIS again poses a threat.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy lawyer raises explosive doubt over who killed her children
item.description: Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington argued for the first time that prosecutors failed to prove she killed her three children.
item.content:encoded:
PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy’s defense lawyer made a surprise shift in strategy Tuesday, according to legal analysts — shifting gears from his argument at trial that she was not criminally responsible because she suffered from postpartum psychosis.

"Where’s the evidence that she did this?" Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, asked Judge William Sullivan in court Tuesday. "Where is the evidence she did this?"

Reddington made the argument while asking Sullivan to enter a not-guilty finding after the jury deadlocked.

LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR ASKS FOR ONE THING IN NEW VIDEO AFTER MISTRIAL DRAMA

"I submit to the court there is no evidence she made any statements, as far as the actual killing of the children, which forms the basis of the indictments," Reddington said.

Plymouth County prosecutors countered, calling his assertion "a laughable argument." But it marked a striking change in the way he's argued the case in the past.

He pointed to what he described as gaps in the physical evidence, including the blood, DNA, timing and circumstances surrounding Clancy’s suicide attempt, which left her paralyzed.

LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON SIGNALS HE'S OPEN TO A DEAL, HOPES DA WILL 'REVISIT' CASE

"For the first time we saw Kevin Reddington say that there’s reasonable doubt as to whether Lindsay Clancy actually killed her children," said former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani, who has been closely following the case. "He's never said that in the courtroom, outside the courtroom — and in fact at the beginning of the first trial, he offered to stipulate to Lindsay killing her three children."

Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after jurors could not agree on a verdict following roughly a week of deliberations. Since then, several jurors have spoken out publicly, describing an 11-1 deadlock with only one man voting to find her guilty of murder.

LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR ADMITTED 'REASONABLE DOUBT' BUT STILL REFUSED INSANITY VERDICT, FOREPERSON SAYS

The 11 sided with Reddington's not guilty due to mental illness or defect defense. He argued that Clancy was not criminally responsible for strangling her children with exercise bands due to postpartum psychosis.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Only one juror voted to convict, and Reddington started calling him an "obstructionist" — first last week when approached by Fox News Digital and again outside the courthouse Tuesday. During the hearing, Reddington also raised concerns about the prosecution’s case and the police investigation launched after Clancy was found in the backyard suffering from injuries that left her paralyzed.

LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS FACE DILEMMA: RETRIAL OR PLEA DEAL IN CASE INVOLVING 3 STRANGLED CHILDREN

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"This may just be a defense lawyer denying everything, using the kitchen sink approach, hoping one of these arguments would resonate with Judge Sullivan," Rahmani said. "Or it could be a shift in defense strategy, where maybe instead of arguing insanity or lack of criminal responsibility at the retrial, they put on a third party culpability defense as well, arguing that maybe someone else is the real killer."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Reddington's comments came during oral arguments on what's called a Rule 25(b)(2) motion — asking Sullivan to override the deadlocked jury and enter a not-guilty finding on the alleged grounds that the Commonwealth's evidence was legally insufficient to garner a conviction.

LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT

Such motions are routine but seldom successful, according to Carol Erskine, a retired Massachusetts judge and child welfare advocate who has been following the case closely.

LINDSAY CLANCY DA RARELY DOES PLEA DEALS, BUT HER CASE COULD BE THE 'EXCEPTION,' VETERAN ATTORNEY SAYS

GOT A TIP?

"He is arguing that [they] did not prove each and every element as required by law," she told Fox News Digital. "I understand why people don’t get this, but he had to argue sufficiency of evidence under Rule 25(b)(2) case law. He told the judge he asked for a Bowden instruction and was denied which meant he was challenging the poor investigation/search at the home by police. It’s a very nuanced argument."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

It's also a different argument than the prior Rule 25 motion that Reddington filed at the end of Clancy's mistrial, which Sullivan denied.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"I will say it was a total surprise that his strategy changed from the original 25(b)(2) motion," Erskine said. "Did not expect it."

LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON FIRES BACK AT LONE HOLDOUT JUROR'S ATTORNEY AFTER FIERY INTERVIEW

Clancy is due back in court on Nov. 2 for another motion hearing. She has pending motions to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds and to open an inquiry into the holdout juror.

A new trial has not yet been scheduled. Both the prosecution and the defense told the court they needed more time, and Reddington said that he's not available to start one until June 2027.

item.title: Inside the neighborhood living on the edge of America’s tech frontier
item.description: Loudoun County homeowners on Statesboro Place describe constant noise from Amazon Web Services and Microsoft data centers just 150 feet from backyards.
item.content:encoded:
ASHBURN, Va. — First came the explosions, the heavy machinery and the red dust that coated the neighborhood. Soon after, towering, windowless buildings emerged just beyond a thin row of trees.

Months after the construction noise faded, the silence gave way to a steady mechanical hum.

For homeowners on the tucked-away cul-de-sac of Statesboro Place in Loudoun County, Virginia, suburban life now shares a fence line with the infrastructure powering America's artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

The facilities behind the neighborhood are operated by Amazon Web Services and Microsoft, two of the world's largest cloud computing companies.

"It's like 150 feet away and just constant noise," one resident told Fox News Digital while looking out over the backyard on a rainy September afternoon. "So far, they've planted some trees, thinking that would solve the issue."

A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES

A Microsoft spokesperson told Fox News Digital the company is "actively meeting with nearby HOAs to address community priorities, including landscaping, lighting and noise, working to ensure that our development lives up to residents' expectations."

An Amazon spokesperson said the company has "been part of Loudoun for 20 years" and that its local team has been working directly with residents and the HOA to address concerns. "We’re committed to building responsibly and being good neighbors," the spokesperson said.

The residents interviewed for this story requested anonymity as they are engaged in ongoing discussions with the HOA and county officials.

One resident, who bought the home nearly a decade ago, said the hum extends beyond the backyards and can be heard along the community's walking trails.

"Only two data centers are active right now and two additional ones are planned to be active next spring," the resident said, adding that neighbors fear the noise will only grow louder.

The neighborhood sits in Loudoun County home to the world's largest concentration of data centers and one of the epicenters of the nation's AI infrastructure buildout. Residents say they were drawn to the spacious lots, unobstructed views and quiet streets, all of which are now overshadowed by featureless buildings.

THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS

As of March 2026, more than 230 data centers had been built or were under construction across the Virginia county, with another 116 projects in the pipeline.

"When I moved in, it was an open field. I had a nice backyard and there was not an ugly building to look at," another resident told Fox News Digital.

The resident says the question isn't whether data centers should exist, but whether they belong so close to neighborhoods without a better understanding of how they affect the people living beside them.

"Are we the guinea pigs? It feels that way."

The data centers that transformed the landscape have also reshaped Loudoun County's finances.

County officials say data centers generated $1.2 billion in tax revenue in fiscal year 2026 — 39% of the county budget — and project that figure will rise to $1.3 billion in fiscal year 2027. The revenue helps fund county services and keep tax rates lower, but residents say their individual bills have continued to rise.

One Loudoun County homeowner shared six years of property tax records with Fox News Digital showing the annual real estate tax bill rose from $17,391 in 2021 to about $22,250 in 2026, an increase of nearly $5,000.

"In our experience, our taxes have not gone down. We also own multiple properties and vehicles in Loudoun County and we have not experienced a reduction in our real estate or personal property tax burden," the homeowner said.

The bill can rise even when tax rates fall if the assessed value increases.

ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM

That disconnect has raised questions about whether the industry’s financial benefits outweigh its impact on nearby communities. Little River District Supervisor Laura TeKrony said Loudoun County should limit data center development to industrial areas.

"I have not voted for one data center application since my term started in 2024," TeKrony told Fox News Digital. "There are some things that matter more than additional tax revenue: our land, our water, our quality of life, and our community character."

AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY

Residents told Fox News Digital they recognize the data centers are unlikely to go away. Instead, they want county leaders and operators to reduce the impact through sound barriers, ongoing noise monitoring and tax relief for homeowners living closest to the facilities.

"Trees are not a solution," one resident said, arguing for a sound wall similar to those installed along major highways.

Another homeowner said nearby residents should receive property tax relief if the county continues approving data centers next to neighborhoods.

"If you ask me what the county can help us with, it's reduce our property tax by at least 50%," the resident said.

So while Americans are hopping the emerging tech boom will not negatively impact them, the nation’s AI ambitions have become impossible to ignore on Statesboro Place.

item.title: Liberal stronghold set to adopt eye-popping minimum wage amid business exodus
item.description: Seattle's minimum wage is set to hit $22.14 in 2027 as 450 restaurants closed in early 2025 and job postings dropped 35% since February 2020.
item.content:encoded:
Seattle is slated to increase its minimum wage to $22.14 an hour in 2027 as the broader metro area contends with a sharp drop in job openings and Seattle businesses face mounting cost pressures.

Beginning in 2025, all Seattle employers, including small businesses, were required to pay the same minimum wage, which is adjusted annually for inflation. Several Seattle restaurant owners who have since closed their businesses have cited rising labor costs among the financial pressures that contributed to their decisions.

During the first half of 2025, shortly after the wage hikes went into effect for all businesses, 450 Seattle restaurants — about 16% of the city’s total — closed. Restaurant and retail transactions fell by as much as 7% over the prior year in some business and shopping districts around Amazon and Microsoft campuses, according to Square data cited by The Wall Street Journal.

SANDERS-AOC BACKED PROGRESSIVE DEBUTS FEDERAL $25 MINIMUM WAGE BILL WITH COALITION OF 100+ ORGANIZATIONS

If no other jurisdictions increase their minimum wages to match or surpass Seattle, the Emerald City will have the highest minimum wage in the country next year. An individual working full time on minimum wage in the city will make just over $46,000 annually.

"If the servers are making $20 an hour, then I gotta pay the cooks $35," one Seattle restaurant owner said of the wage increases to Eater in 2024.

LA HOTEL LEADERS WARN MAYOR BASS' $30 WAGE MANDATE IS KILLING BUSINESS AHEAD OF WORLD CUP, OLYMPICS

"Operators are making less money than ever and are charging more than ever," Anthony Anton, CEO of the Washington Hospitality Association, said last year, according to the Center Square.

A peer-reviewed study published by researchers at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, found that the mere announcement of Seattle’s minimum wage increase decreased the formation of new businesses in city limits while actually increasing the founding of new businesses in adjacent suburbs with lower wage floors.

Proponents of Seattle's minimum wage increase, however, argue that the city's high cost of living necessitates higher pay for those on the lower end of the economic spectrum to avoid more people falling into poverty. They also claim that higher pay can help businesses with staff retention.

DOWNTOWN SEATTLE LOST 30,000 JOBS, BILLIONS IN OFFICE VALUE SINCE 2020 PAYROLL TAX: NEW REPORT FINDS

Seattle's degrading business environment predates the widespread implementation of its inflation-indexed minimum wage laws.

From the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020 to 2023, about 500 local businesses closed, according to the Downtown Seattle Association. A year later, the association counted 543 vacant storefronts in the city. During this period, many business owners cited property crime as well as local economic factors as the reasoning behind their exits.

Declining business formation comes at an inopportune time for Seattle residents as job postings in the city’s metropolitan area fell by 35% between February 2020 and October 2025, a decline second only to San Francisco, according to an Axios analysis. Local business owners have reported that individuals with master's degrees, and those with experience at prestigious companies such as Microsoft, are applying to work as baristas.

Seattle’s once-booming tech-driven economy is now showing clear signs of strain, from weaker hiring to elevated downtown office vacancies.

As of the fourth quarter of 2025, 35.6% of Seattle’s downtown office space was vacant, up from 32.3% the year before, according to Cushman & Wakefield data. Some iconic Seattle businesses, Starbucks, for example, have shifted operations away from the city.

item.title: US faces another major Middle East troop withdrawal, but threat remains
item.description: About 2,500 U.S. troops had remained in Iraq as part of Operation Inherent Resolve, but Baghdad's effort to disarm Iran-backed militias remains unfinished.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. military is scheduled to end its mission in Iraq on Wednesday, bringing to a close a military operation that has lasted more than two decades — despite an ongoing war in Iran sparked earlier this year.

The Iraq mission began with the 2003 invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein and later evolved into a campaign to help Iraqi forces defeat the Islamic State group after the terrorist organization's rapid rise across Iraq and Syria.

In recent years, however, the remaining U.S. military presence has increasingly served as both a counterweight to Iran's influence and a frequent target of Iran-backed militias.

The Iraq agreement was reached before the U.S. and Iran entered direct conflict earlier this year and under a different administration and military leadership — leaving the final phase of the withdrawal to unfold in a dramatically different security environment than the one envisioned when the timeline was negotiated.

TRUMP REVEALS WHEN US MILITARY WILL LEAVE IRAQ AFTER 23-YEAR MISSION

The deadline stems from an agreement reached by Washington and Baghdad in 2024 under President Joe Biden to wind down the U.S.-led coalition's military mission after Iraqi officials concluded their security forces were increasingly capable of handling the fight against ISIS.

It follows the U.S. military's 2021 departure from Afghanistan, also under the Biden administration, which ended another two-decade American war and left no U.S. troops in the country. The withdrawal, however, was chaotic, widely viewed as 'botched' and resulted in the deaths of 13 U.S. service members and dozens of civilians.

HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY

The Pentagon declined to confirm to Fox News Digital whether the timeline remains on track or provide details about any continuing U.S. military involvement in Iraq after Wednesday. The Iraqi Embassy did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The danger to U.S. forces persisted through the final months of the mission. Army Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, was killed at Erbil Air Base in July during the controlled detonation of a downed Iranian attack drone.

About 2,500 U.S. troops had remained in Iraq as part of Operation Inherent Resolve, the U.S.-led coalition established in 2014 after ISIS seized large swaths of Iraq and Syria. American forces had previously withdrawn from Iraq in 2011 before returning three years later to help Iraqi and partner forces combat the terrorist group.

That threat has since diminished significantly.

The Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) assessed this summer that ISIS in Iraq "almost certainly remains severely degraded," focused largely on its own survival and unable to capitalize on instability from the war with Iran, according to the latest Lead Inspector General report on Operation Inherent Resolve.

CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper told lawmakers in May that ISIS attacks in Iraq and Syria had fallen 70% since 2023 and were at their lowest level since 2013.

The U.S. mission had already shifted accordingly. Rather than routinely fighting alongside Iraqi forces, American troops increasingly trained, advised and provided intelligence to local forces expected to carry out counterterrorism operations with limited or no direct U.S. involvement.

The Pentagon also began moving the infrastructure for that fight out of Iraq. Operation Inherent Resolve shifted its headquarters to Amman, Jordan, this year, allowing U.S. personnel and assets to redeploy while Iraqi forces assumed greater responsibility for counterterrorism operations.

But the declining ISIS threat has coincided with a different challenge for Baghdad: powerful Iran-backed armed groups that have resisted efforts to surrender their weapons.

US-BACKED EFFORT TO DISARM IRAQ’S IRAN-LINKED MILITIAS HITS SETBACK, EXPERTS SAY

The Iraqi government had initially sought to bring armed groups operating outside state control to heel by the same Sept. 30 deadline. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi argued that the departure of U.S. forces would eliminate a key justification for the militias to remain armed.

Several powerful Iran-backed groups, however, have resisted calls to disarm. Two prominent factions initially agreed to surrender their weapons by the deadline, while other armed groups refused, according to a U.S. government report released this summer.

Baghdad has since pushed back its timeline. Zaidi said last week that the government now aims to complete the process by June 30, 2027, beginning with a 90-day period in which armed groups would halt attacks in exchange for assurances that U.S. forces would not target them. The groups would then gradually surrender their weapons or be brought under state control.

The holdouts remain heavily armed. U.S. military officials said the groups retain rockets, missiles, drones and, in some cases, air defense systems capable of threatening American personnel and facilities across the region.

The DIA reported that Iran-aligned militias launched hundreds of attacks on U.S. forces and diplomatic facilities in Iraq after the war with Iran began.

That leaves the end of the U.S. mission arriving as the threat that brought American forces back to Iraq has substantially diminished, while Baghdad's effort to disarm some of the groups that have targeted those forces remains unfinished.

item.title: 'Lost' medieval castle found hiding in plain sight after professor spots telltale clues
item.description: A University College Dublin professor found that up to 80% of the medieval Roebuck Castle is still intact beneath Victorian plaster on the modern campus.
item.content:encoded:
A professor recently discovered that a medieval castle thought to have been lost for centuries was hiding in plain sight — inside a Victorian-era building on a modern college campus.

The discovery was announced by University College Dublin (UCD), in Dublin, Ireland, on Sept. 18.

The school announced in a release — entitled "'Lost' medieval castle found hiding inside UCD building" — that medieval archaeology professor Tadhg O'Keeffe found substantial portions of the medieval Roebuck Castle still survive within the university's present-day building.

DISCOVERY BENEATH SOCCER FIELD REVEALS MASSIVE MEDIEVAL CONVENT LOST FOR CENTURIES

The present-day Roebuck Castle retained the name of its medieval predecessor — but the Victorian-looking building was long believed to contain little, if any, of the original castle.

The original structure had fallen into ruin by the 18th century and was later incorporated into a residence that underwent extensive alterations, including a major Victorian makeover in 1874. UCD purchased the property in 1986.

O'Keeffe told Fox News Digital that, despite those centuries of changes, most of the medieval structure is still there.

"I would say that 70 to 80% of the building is still there, hidden under Victorian plaster," he said.

He began investigating after studying 18th-century watercolors by artist Gabriel Beranger, which depicted the medieval castle before the property underwent major redevelopment.

1,000-YEAR-OLD CHURCH MYSTERY CRACKED BY STUDENTS FROM KING CHARLES' ALMA MATER

"I wasn't terribly optimistic," O'Keeffe said. "When I got into the building and had a look around, I realized that actually, most of the castle is still there, inside the building.

"It's not obvious to the naked eye," he went on. "It's not obvious to a non-expert. But I specialize in medieval castle architecture, and I saw all the indications when I went in that the castle is still there."

The clues were hiding beneath the building's more modern appearance.

O'Keeffe pointed to unusually thick walls, along with a stone vault and arched stone roof, as evidence of the building's medieval past.

"The gate tower is very clear on the inside," he said.

FIRST-EVER IMAGES REVEAL MYSTERIOUS REMAINS OF TOWN SWALLOWED BY SEA 700 YEARS AGO

"Everything is plastered over so you can't see the original stonework anymore, but it's all clearly still there," he said. "Also, the windows are splayed, and splayed windows are a real indication of a medieval date."

Roebuck Castle was likely built in the early 13th century, after the Norman invasion of Ireland began in the late 12th century.

Roebuck Castle also stands out for another reason: Researchers know who owned it through much of the Middle Ages.

The owners were "people of some significance," O'Keeffe added.

HIDDEN UNDERGROUND CHAMBER REVEALED BENEATH HOME OF LEGENDARY ROMAN EMPEROR

"One of them, in modern terms, would be the equivalent of the chief justice in the Supreme Court, the most senior legal person in Ireland for part of the Middle Ages," the historian said.

"Another resident at one stage, temporarily, was King James II. It's reputed that he lived there briefly in the late 1600s."

That level of detail is unusual, O'Keeffe said, because records for castles around Dublin are generally sparse.

"We have a record of its owners really until about the start of the 17th century, when it seems to have been abandoned and probably suffered in the wars of the mid-17th century," he said. "So it's unusual for a castle of its type to have a recorded history."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Although the renovations preserved much of the medieval castle, O'Keeffe said, it appears to have been more a matter of practicality than historic preservation.

"There was no policy of preservation. There was not a particular interest in the medieval building," he said.

"They clearly figured that the fastest way to do that was to simply leave those walls and incorporate them."

O'Keeffe said the discovery suggests other castles in Ireland that are presumed lost could still survive within later buildings.

"The great takeaway ... is never assume things are gone," he said. "You have to go in and look. You have to explore."

"There are probably lots of other castles that are locked up in buildings around the country [and] are assumed to be gone — but are not gone at all," he said.

item.title: Flydubai pilots reportedly fight in cockpit, triggering hijacking fears and Israeli fighter jet response
item.description: A Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia Wednesday after a reported cockpit fight between pilots triggered hijacking fears in Israel.
item.content:encoded:
A Flydubai flight headed for Israel made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia Wednesday after a reported fight between the pilots triggered a distress alert, raising fears of a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble fighter jets.

The Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and everyone aboard was reported safe, according to officials.

A regional official briefed on the incident said an altercation broke out in the cockpit and apparently involved the pilots, though it was not immediately clear what sparked the confrontation. Israeli media, citing security officials, also reported that a dispute between the two pilots was behind the emergency.

The incident prompted an immediate security response in Israel, where authorities initially feared the plane — carrying dozens of Israeli citizens — could have been hijacked. A second official confirmed that Israel scrambled fighter jets as the situation unfolded.

MIDAIR SCARE FORCES PACKED PASSENGER JET INTO EMERGENCY LANDING, TRAVELERS HOSPITALIZED

The aircraft transmitted an emergency alert during the flight, according to publicly available flight-tracking information. Flight FZ1073 had departed Dubai and was headed for Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv before diverting to Tabuk.

Passengers described a tense scene aboard the aircraft as the emergency unfolded. Travelers told Israel's Channel 12 by phone that they heard shouting from passengers near the front of the plane who had apparently heard the cockpit altercation. They also said the aircraft dipped steeply before landing in Saudi Arabia.

AMERICANS WARNED AGAINST TRAVEL PLANS AS TERRORISM THREATENS POPULAR DESTINATION

After landing, passengers remained aboard the plane as a heavy Saudi security presence surrounded the aircraft, according to their accounts to the Israeli outlet.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office later said the situation was under control and that Israeli authorities were working to bring the passengers home. The scare came as Netanyahu has warned in recent days about unspecified heightened security threats facing Israel.

Flydubai later confirmed that FZ1073 had experienced an incident while traveling to Ben Gurion Airport and landed safely in Tabuk.

"Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities," the carrier said. "Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available."

The exact circumstances surrounding the reported cockpit confrontation remained unclear Wednesday.

While disputes between pilots serious enough to affect a flight are rare, similar incidents have occurred. Two Air France pilots were suspended in 2022 after fighting in the cockpit during a flight from Geneva to Paris. That aircraft did not divert and landed as scheduled.

The initial hijacking fears carried particular weight in Israel, where aviation security has long been shaped by a history of attacks on Israeli travelers and aircraft. Palestinian militants carried out a series of hijackings and attacks involving Israelis during the 1960s and 1970s. Israel has not experienced an aircraft hijacking in decades and maintains stringent security procedures for Israel-bound flights.

Flydubai is a lower-cost sister carrier of Emirates. Flights between Israel and the United Arab Emirates began after the two countries normalized relations in 2020, opening the UAE as a major destination for Israeli travelers.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: LEE CARTER: Trump can still get attention, can he distract voters from their bills?
item.description: Trump's approval on inflation sits at just 24% as polls show 62% of voters call grocery prices a major problem ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has never suffered from an attention deficit.

Ours, maybe. His, never.

For more than a decade, Trump has demonstrated an almost supernatural ability to decide what America will talk about. A nickname. A Truth Social post. A feud. A rally. A tariff. A threat. A late-night broadside against somebody who had the gall to criticize him.

TO WIN IN NOVEMBER, REPUBLICANS NEED TO TAKE A PAGE FROM OBAMA’S PLAYBOOK

Trump throws the ball and Washington and the media chase it.

But something interesting is happening as we head toward the midterms.

REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY.

The country may be getting tired of chasing.

The latest Fox News poll contains a number that should be flashing in giant red letters inside the White House: Asked, without being given a list, to name the most important issue facing the country, 34% of registered voters said the cost of living. Another 14% said the economy and jobs.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: WHAT’S IN AN ECONOMY?

Nothing else came close. Immigration was at 8%. The war with Iran, 4%. AI and data centers, despite consuming approximately 94% of the oxygen in corporate America, registered at 1%.

Voters are not being subtle.

IT’S NOT THE ECONOMY, STUPID. AMERICANS VOTE BASED ON THEIR PERSONAL ECONOMY

They are saying: It's the prices. Stupid.

And yet much of the political conversation seems to be happening somewhere else.

REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE

Trump is battling the media. He is talking about his predecessor. He is dealing with Iran, China, immigration and AI. Some of those issues are enormously consequential. Presidents do not get to spend their days staring at the price of eggs.

But voters don't experience the presidency as a policy seminar.

RECORD GAS PRICES SQUEEZE AMERICANS AS SUMMER TRAVEL SEASON ENDS, MIDTERMS LOOM AND IRAN WAR WAGES ON

They experience it at the grocery store.

At the gas pump.

THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE

When the utility bill arrives.

When they look at what it costs to buy a house, see a doctor or fill their grocery cart.

BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT

And on those questions, the Fox numbers are difficult for the administration. Sixty-two percent say grocery prices are a major problem. Sixty-one percent say the same about gas prices. Fifty-four percent say it about housing. Fifty-two percent about health care. And 63% say the Trump administration has made the economy worse.

The administration can point to its own economic strength data. Employment has remained resilient, and the stock market has performed strongly. Fox's own analysis recently noted job growth and unemployment of 4.1%.

But this is where presidents (and politicians writ large) discover one of the more irritating rules of politics:

You don't get to tell voters how they feel about the economy.

They tell you.

That was true for President Joe Biden. It is true for Donald Trump.

Biden spent much of his presidency pointing to macroeconomic statistics that were considerably healthier than the public mood. Inflation was coming down. Jobs were being created. The economy had avoided the recession many economists predicted.

And voters kept saying some version of: That's lovely. Do you know how much a dozen eggs cost?

Trump understood that disconnect better than almost anyone. He turned economic frustration into political fuel. Now he owns the podium. Which means he also owns the problem.

A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found only 17% of U.S. adults approved of Trump's handling of the cost of living. His overall approval was 32% in that survey. Fox, polling registered voters with a different methodology, put his overall approval at 39% and his approval on inflation at 24%. Different polls, different populations, same warning light: affordability is a major vulnerability for the administration.

This is where Trump's greatest communications strength can become a weakness. He understands attention better than perhaps any political figure of the modern era. He knows how to interrupt. He knows how to provoke. He knows how to make himself the main character. But attention and persuasion are not the same thing.

Attention is getting everyone to look at you.

Persuasion is getting them to look at the problem differently.

And right now, voters appear to have a problem they don't particularly want changed. They want it solved.

There is another revealing number buried in the Fox poll. Democrats currently hold a 15-point advantage over Republicans when voters are asked which party they trust more on inflation. But the same poll offers an important qualification: voters who trust Democrats on inflation are slightly more likely to say it is because Republicans have failed than because they believe Democratic policies will lower prices. That isn't exactly a love letter to either party. It's an eviction notice to whoever voters think isn't listening. And that's why the midterm communications challenge may be simpler than Washington is making it.

Trump doesn't need another subject. He has one. Affordability. Every other argument can run through it.

China? What does competing with China mean for American jobs and prices?

AI? What does it mean for my paycheck and electric bill?

Iran? What does a prolonged conflict mean for gasoline and the cost of moving goods around the country?

Taxes and tariffs? What will I pay?

The communications opportunity isn't necessarily to talk less about the world. It's to translate the world into the lives people are actually living. Trump's political genius has always been his instinct for finding the thing people are feeling before the political establishment figures out how to talk about it.

In 2016, that was disruption.

In 2024, it was frustration with prices, immigration and the direction of the country.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

In 2026, voters are once again telling Washington exactly what's bothering them.

The question is whether Washington is listening. Trump can still make America look. The harder task now is convincing Americans that he's looking at what they're looking at.

item.title: Schumer preaches affordability in Dem midterm pitch while sabotaging GOP fixes for soaring costs
item.description: Senate Democrats blocked GOP affordability and permitting reform bills, raising questions about their campaign messaging on cost of living issues.
item.content:encoded:
Democrats are pitching themselves as the answer to the economic woes Americans are facing in their pursuit of power in Congress, but they have made a habit of blocking the GOP’s attempts to tackle cost of living issues.

Affordability has become the centerpiece of the Democrats' campaign messaging heading into Election Day in November, and they’ve wielded it like a political cudgel that left-wing candidates from Michigan to Texas are using to browbeat Republicans.

But in the Senate, it requires cooperation and compromise to tackle those issues, and Republicans say that their colleagues across the aisle have bedeviled that process. They’ll have one last shot Wednesday to address a sliver of the issue with a bill targeting data centers and voters' pocketbooks, but Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his caucus are poised to block it.

FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY

"I think right now, the whole thing is just, you know, play politics with all these issues and get to the election," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital. "I think that, you know, what you're seeing is that this is the party of no, can't take yes for an answer, and is interested in just trying to politicize everything going into the election."

When asked if blocking the data center bill, and another that would ban members of Congress from trading stocks, could turn the table on Democrats’ messaging, Thune said "Well, it makes it pretty hard for Democrats to make that argument."

Democrats don’t believe that blocking the bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, would hurt their affordability message, particularly because the legislation lacks teeth — many of the requirements for large-load customers, like data centers, to repay their electricity usage are optional.

Schumer trashed the data center bill as being purely politically motivated to bolster a vulnerable candidate staring down a tough race in November against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, even though only three House Democrats voted against it earlier this month.

ANXIETY GROWS OVER EMERGING ELECTION ISSUE, BUT GOP SAYS WASHINGTON ISN'T THE ANSWER

"Because we don't vote for frauds," Schumer said when asked why Senate Democrats wouldn't vote for it. "It's voluntary. Not a single company has to comply with it."

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., told Fox News Digital that if "you guys do your job and explain that the the bill does nothing," the political ramifications would be low for Democrats.

"It does nothing, and so people know that, but there's more political risk for them than for us," Murphy said.

When asked if there was a concern that shutting the bill down could hamper their best weapon on the campaign trail, Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital, "Absolutely not."

"The American people can see through just the politics of this. They know that this bill is good for Senator Husted, but not necessarily for them, because it's not — it doesn't have anything that would actually force change," Kim said.

REPUBLICANS FEAR THEY ‘HAVEN’T DONE A DAMN THING’ TO LOWER PRICES AHEAD OF MIDTERM RECKONING

Not all Democrats want to outright kill the GOP’s latest affordability push, however.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., isn’t totally against allowing the legislation to proceed, but he wants a guarantee from Thune that his bill, the Power for the People Act, would get an amendment vote to add some regulatory heft to the measure.

"You want to address the affordability issue, you need to do something real," Van Hollen told Fox News Digital. "As soon as Senator Thune says he'll have a vote on Power for the People Act, then for sure, we should go forward."

It’s not the only attempt at grappling with affordability issues that Democrats have sunk, or at least kneecapped, near the finish line before the midterms.

Republican leaders wanted to get a deal on permitting reform, which would lower costs on energy projects and reform the regulatory process writ large, on the floor during this final sprint before the election, but Democrats walked away from the deal last week.

"I would tell you, all the chemistry, I think, was perfect for getting this deal done," Sen. Alan Armstrong, R-Okla., who has led the permitting reform push told Fox News Digital. "And that doesn't happen very often on such a complex issue. So it's very disappointing."

The deal is reportedly back on, but won’t be handled until after the election during Congress’ lame duck period, where several agenda items have been punted that may never see the light of day.

Still, Republicans will need Democrats to get anything post-election, and the track record of bipartisanship over the near two years that they’ve controlled the chamber has ebbed and flowed.

"I mean, we got 53 Republicans, you got to have 60. I’d have busted the filibuster a long time ago and we would've had a lot more done," Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., told Fox News Digital. "But we wasted a year and a half of President Trump."

item.title: MAHA moms are still up for grabs this election. They want more than cheap groceries
item.description: RFK Jr. has scored early wins on food additives and ultra-processed foods, but the GOP's stance on glyphosate and PFAS has frustrated MAHA moms.
item.content:encoded:
November is looming, and Republicans are eager to turn out every voter that propelled them to victory in 2024. A critical part of their winning coalition was the "MAHA moms," a group that doesn’t neatly fit into either party but cares deeply about food safety, public health and a clean environment.

President Trump won this group in 2024 largely by joining forces with RFK Jr., who is, according to some polls, currently the most popular member of the Trump administration. But there’s no guarantee these voters will stick with the GOP. If Republicans want to drive MAHA mom turnout, they need to champion a winning environmental-health agenda.

Ultimately, MAHA moms don’t just want to be able to afford food for their families. They want to afford good food. Because raising healthy kids shouldn’t require being rich.

TRUMP TO NOMINATE DR HEIDI OVERTON AS NEXT FDA COMMISSIONER

Moms across the socioeconomic spectrum have started reading ingredient labels, worrying about pesticides, cutting out food dyes and filtering water. RFK Jr. isn’t popular because he gets everything right, but because he was the first political leader in a long time to confront the chronic disease epidemic and question why half of the ingredients on the average loaf of bread were only intelligible to a small subset of food scientists.

RFK Jr. has had initial successes. The administration has proposed closing the decades-old loophole that allowed food companies to introduce new chemicals without telling the FDA.

HHS and USDA also submitted the government's first proposed definition of ultra-processed foods, which make up nearly 60% of the American diet.

And most recently, the EPA announced a cutting-edge study screening drinking water for over 1,400 emerging contaminants, including PFAS, pesticides, pharmaceuticals and the abortion-inducing mifepristone. For MAHA moms, these are tangible signs that someone in Washington is finally listening.

BROOKE ROLLINS, DR. BEN CARSON: WE ARE PUTTING REAL FOOD BACK ON SCHOOL LUNCH TRAYS

But, progress on one front has come with frustration on another. The same administration that is scrutinizing food additives has moved to protect glyphosate, the herbicide found in Roundup and the most widely used weed killer in American agriculture that some fear is carcinogenic. When the Supreme Court heard arguments in a major Roundup liability case this spring, the Trump administration filed a brief on behalf of the pesticide's manufacturer. RFK Jr. largely sidestepped questions about the administration's pesticide stance when pressed by Congress.

Meanwhile, under Administrator Zeldin's deregulatory agenda, the EPA has moved to roll back drinking water standards for PFAS and weakened protections against mercury and other air pollutants.

MAHA moms are not naive about this tension. They are thankful their concerns are finally part of the national conversation. Likewise, they are wary of the left’s heavy-handed government policies that have failed to improve public health while making life unaffordable. But, they haven’t yet been convinced that the GOP actually wants to respond to their concerns rather than check a few boxes.

If Republicans want to build a sustainable coalition around MAHA, they need more than ad hoc wins. They need a distinctly conservative environmental and health agenda, one that takes the constituency's concerns seriously without defaulting to the assumption that another layer of federal regulation will fix them.

REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE

That balance is not impossible. It starts by applying the conservative principles of private-sector initiative, deregulation, light-touch intervention to environmental concerns.

Take farmers. Many are trapped in a system that pays them to lean on pesticides and synthetic fertilizers they'd rather not use. A conservative agricultural agenda could eliminate perverse subsidies that entrench chemical dependency while creating new incentives for regenerative farming practices that produce cleaner food, healthier soil, and better farm economics, all without a Washington bureaucrat telling farmers how to do their jobs.

BROOKE ROLLINS, MONICA CROWLEY: AMERICA’S FAMILY FARMS HAVE KEPT US STRONG FOR 250 YEARS

The same logic extends to energy, and it leads straight back to the grocery bill. Fresh food is expensive in part because it is energy-hungry. It has to be grown, processed, refrigerated, and trucked, and kept cold the whole way to the shelf. Whole ingredients and minimally processed foods, the kind MAHA moms are trying to buy, are among the most exposed to those costs. Cheaper, more abundant power brings them down at every step.

Relatedly, the private sector, not a Green New Deal, is driving a historic solar buildout that has the technology on track to become the world's largest source of power by 2035. The Trump administration's deregulation of nuclear energy points the same direction. It’s one of the cleanest and most reliable sources available, delivering cleaner air and a steadier grid without the intermittency problems of wind and solar. For farmers, processors, and grocers alike, that means lower operating costs, and for families it means the difference between good food as a luxury and good food as the default.

GOP HANDED NEW LIFELINE ON BIGGEST POCKETBOOK FIGHT OF MIDTERMS

None of these things are left-wing ideas. They apply the logic of conservatism to the health and environmental issues that matter to millions of voters.

Republicans have a narrow window to win over MAHA moms with a conservative agenda that takes environmental health concerns seriously. If the GOP answers the call, it will pay dividends not just in the midterms, but in the elections to come.

item.title: How Ms Rachel's political activism is sparking pushback from parents
item.description: Rachel Accurso, known as Ms. Rachel, pledged to match Macklemore's $1 million donation to the Palestine Children's Relief Fund amid backlash.
item.content:encoded:
At first glance, Rachel Accurso, better known by her persona Ms. Rachel, looks like your typical toddler entertainer clad in denim overalls, a pink T-shirt and a matching headband. However, Accurso has been at the center of political controversies, which heightened as she began talking about the situation in Gaza as the war between Israel and Hamas unfolded. The children's entertainer has been accused of amplifying Hamas data and elevating narratives that have proven to be false.

Recently, Accurso voiced her support for rapper Macklemore, who was dropped from Ed Sheeran's "Loop Tour" after he repeatedly called for a "Free Palestine" and performed his anti-Israel song "Hind's Hall" during his opening act at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

Macklemore announced he would donate the $1 million he earned from the tour to organizations aiding Palestinians. Accurso later announced that she would match the rapper's $1 million donation, giving it to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, an organization for which she is an ambassador.

In one of her more famous controversies, Accurso called Palestinian photojournalist Motaz Azaiza her "friend" in a 2025 video. The clip was taken just days before Azaiza admitted that he hid footage of Israeli hostages being beaten by a crowd in Gaza on Oct. 7, 2023. He told an Arabic-language podcast he hid the footage over concerns that it would put the Palestinians involved in the beatings at risk. Accurso later deleted the video, though clips have resurfaced since its original publication.

MS RACHEL URGES 'EVERY WEALTHY WHITE CELEBRITY' TO MATCH MACKLEMORE'S DONATION TO PALESTINIAN CAUSES

When speaking to the Guardian, Accurso addressed her choice to take political stands, saying that she has "a really good moral compass."

"This is the case for a lot of liberals," Bethany Mandel, a Washington Examiner contributor, author and homeschooling mom of six, told Fox News Digital. "They don't see it as a political perspective at all. They just see the world in black and white and what they are doing is so clearly correct."

Mandel argues that this mindset comes from creators who rarely step outside their ideological "bubble" to engage with those who hold opposing beliefs.

When it comes to issues such as the war in Gaza, Mandel believes this dynamic becomes particularly dangerous, with some adopting a singular narrative and platforming controversial numbers, sometimes supplied by Hamas-run agencies.

"It's important to understand that she only cares about one narrative. She only cares about this very false narrative where what's happening in Gaza is a genocide, falsely categorizing it as such," Mandel said of Accurso. "She amplifies numbers that are not real, the numbers of deceased children, the numbers of people who have died in general, she's accepting a Hamas narrative on every single thing and amplifying it."

MS RACHEL CONFRONTED ON ACCUSING ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' IN PARK INTERACTION WITH PODCASTER

Accurso's controversies have gone beyond her content and into the comment section of her posts. In January 2026, she drew scrutiny after appearing to "like" a comment that read "free America from the Jews."

Accurso explained that she meant to delete the comment, but "accidentally hit like and hide," according to the Jerusalem Post. The outlet noted that in response to her apology post, an account titled "thepalestinenewsnetwork" wrote, "Spoiler alert: They left the comment themselves." Accurso replied "ooooooooooohhhhh," but the comment was later deleted.

"She is serving as their mouthpiece for a lot of Americans not just children and not just the adults that follow her," Mandel told Fox News Digital.

While Accurso's politics became more publicly scrutinized after she began speaking about Gaza, Mandel contends that it's not the first issue on which the children's entertainer took a left-leaning stance. Mandel said that she realized Accurso "cares more about activism than education" when the children's entertainer had a non-binary musician as a guest. While Mandel did not specify the musician's name, it was likely Jules Hoffman, who was known for making videos with Accurso.

"She's had fellow musicians and performers on camera with her who have no gender, and she takes away gender from these individuals especially, and they are amorphous, they go by they/them. And it's a woman, but you can't really tell that, especially as a child," Mandel told Fox News Digital.

MS RACHEL CLAIMS CELEBRITIES SILENT ON GAZA WOULD ‘PROBABLY’ SPEAK IF CHILDREN ‘WERE WHITE’

"And this is something that's really very damaging to children who are in the early stages of development, because one of the first ways that children learn to organize the world around them is by categorization, and the easiest way for a toddler to categorize the world around them is by female and male."

Mandel said that the erasure of gender for young children is something that could potentially have "detrimental consequences."

"This is what Donald Rumsfeld talked about, the unknown unknowns," Mandel explained, noting that altering foundational development markers are uncharted territory when it comes to early childhood education and socialization. "When we take that ability to categorize away from children, we've never done that in human history before. And it absolutely will have detrimental consequences to how they order the world around them, and we're just going to have to find out what those consequences are."

While not all parents may be concerned with gender representation or disagree with Accurso's commentary on Gaza, Mandel argues that for most families, it's only a matter of time before the children's entertainer crosses a line.

"Parents need to choose these entertainers wisely because perhaps parents don't care about the gender stuff, perhaps parents don't care about what she's saying about Gaza, but if they are not ultra-ultra-liberal, Ms. Rachel will eventually land on something that they do feel discomfort with," she told Fox News Digital.

Mandel urges parents to carefully screen everything before they show it to their kids, something that she does for her own children. As for Mandel's household, Ms. Rachel did not pass the test. Mandel told Fox News Digital that years ago she removed Accurso's channel from her family's YouTube playlist, a decision that has given her peace of mind.

"I feel relieved as a Jewish parent that I took Ms. Rachel off of our playlist on YouTube years ago, and I'm sure I will continue to feel great about that decision in the years to come," Mandel said.

Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for Accurso to request comment.

item.title: Maine Dem Sen candidate's 'working class' cred shredded by both parties when internet sees latest 'cringey' ad
item.description: Troy Jackson's boba tea ad mocking Susan Collins and Elon Musk has been viewed over 2 million times, drawing sharp bipartisan ridicule on X.
item.content:encoded:
Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger who has touted his working-class bonafides on the campaign trail, is facing backlash from both sides of the aisle over a viral ad that critics are labeling as tone-deaf pandering. 

"If Republicans spend $46 million on these TV ads, who’s gunna be convinced by that?" Jackson is asked in the ad as he sips a boba tea.

Jackson then looks around and smiles before saying "the 1%ers" as a photo of his opponent, Sen. Susan Collins, and Tesla CEO Elon Musk are shown on the screen.

The ad’s caption reads "sips boba tea" alongside a boba and wide-eyed emoji.

SUSAN COLLINS TEARS INTO BRIBERY ALLEGATIONS AS NEW CLAIMS EMERGE DURING CRITICAL SENATE BATTLE

The ad’s post on X was widely mocked by Democrats and Republicans and has been viewed over 2 million times.

"Maine is the oldest median age electorate in the nation," Democratic strategist Steve Schale posted on X. "I know I’m not a DC strategist but I really, really don’t get it."

"Troy Jackson needs to win but videos like this are unhelpful and cringey," liberal influencer Harry Sisson posted on X. "Please change it up! No boba tea!"

"The same people that ran Mallory McMorrow's campaign into the ground are telling you to do this goofy s---," left-wing podcaster Kyle Kulinski posted on X. "Just get out there and tell the truth and speak from the heart for economic justice and against war and stop with all this bulls---. C'mon man. You're smarter than this."

DEM SENATE NOMINEE BREAKS SILENCE AFTER SUSAN COLLINS' OFFICE WAS VANDALIZED WITH VULGAR MESSAGE

"It's a little bit funny to be desperately trying to position as working class masculine male and have gen-z women run your socials like they would run their own personals," Republican communicator Matt Whitlock posted on X.

"... ," National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) Southern regional press secretary Reilly Richardson posted on X.
